outline.point: Variables, basic data types, and control flow (if/else, loops)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a script that loops through a list of numbers and prints whether each is even or odd.

outline.point: Core data structures: lists, dictionaries, tuples, sets
outline.practicePrompt: Create a dictionary mapping 5 product names to prices, then write code that finds the most expensive product.

outline.point: Functions, default/keyword arguments, and basic error handling (try/except)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a function that divides two numbers and uses try/except to handle division by zero gracefully.

outline.point: Object-oriented basics: classes, objects, and type annotations
outline.practicePrompt: Write a small class 'Message' with typed attributes (role: str, content: str) and a method that prints a formatted version.

outline.point: Working with JSON: parsing and constructing JSON payloads
outline.practicePrompt: Write a script that loads a JSON string into a Python dict, modifies one field, and dumps it back to a JSON string.

outline.point: Asynchronous execution basics: async/await for non-blocking API calls
outline.practicePrompt: Write an async function that simulates two independent 'API calls' (using asyncio.sleep) and runs them concurrently with asyncio.gather.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: mutable vs immutable types, and list/dict comprehensions
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why a list is mutable but a tuple is not, then rewrite a for-loop that filters even numbers as a one-line list comprehension.

name: Basic DSA for AI Engineering Interviews

outline.point: Time/space complexity intuition (Big-O) without deep formal analysis
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in plain language, why searching a Python list is O(n) but looking up a value in a dictionary is close to O(1).

outline.point: Array and string manipulation basics (traversal, slicing, reversing)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a function that reverses a string and another that finds the most frequent word in a list of strings.

outline.point: Using dictionaries/hash maps for frequency counting (a very common pattern)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a function that counts the frequency of each token in a list of strings using a dictionary.

outline.point: Basic recursion (factorial, simple tree/graph traversal concepts as used in agent/graph frameworks)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in your own words, why understanding basic recursion helps when reading a LangGraph-style agent workflow that loops and branches.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: 'two sum' style array problems and why they show up even in AI-focused interviews
outline.practicePrompt: Solve the 'two sum' problem (find two numbers in a list that add to a target) using a dictionary in O(n) time.

outline.point: SELECT, WHERE, and filtering rows
outline.practicePrompt: Write 3 SELECT queries against a sample 'documents' table filtering by different conditions.

outline.point: JOINs and aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, GROUP BY)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a query that joins a 'users' table with a 'queries' table and counts how many queries each user made.

outline.point: INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and basic schema design for logging AI interactions
outline.practicePrompt: Design a simple table schema for logging LLM prompts and responses (columns: id, prompt, response, tokens_used, timestamp), then write an INSERT statement for one row.

outline.point: Working with a Postgres extension for vectors (pgvector) at a conceptual level
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in your own words, what pgvector adds to a normal PostgreSQL database and why an AI engineer might choose it over a dedicated vector database.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: writing a query to retrieve the most recent N records per user (a common pattern for chat history)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a SQL query using window functions to retrieve the 5 most recent chat messages for each user in a messages table.

outline.point: Basic Git workflow: init, add, commit, status, log
outline.practicePrompt: Initialize a Git repository for a small Python script, and make 3 separate commits as you build it out.

outline.point: Branching and merging
outline.practicePrompt: Create a branch for an experimental prompt-tuning change, commit it, and merge it back into main.

outline.point: Working with remotes: clone, push, pull, and pull requests
outline.practicePrompt: Clone a public GitHub repository containing a sample LangChain project, make a small change, and push it to your own fork.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: git merge vs git rebase
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between git merge and git rebase, and when you'd prefer rebase for a feature branch.

outline.point: HTTP basics: methods (GET/POST), status codes, and JSON request/response bodies
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between a GET and a POST request, and describe when you'd use each for an AI service endpoint.

outline.point: Building a basic FastAPI app: routes, path parameters, and request bodies
outline.practicePrompt: Build a FastAPI endpoint POST /summarize that accepts a JSON body with a 'text' field and returns a mock summary string.

outline.point: Request validation using Pydantic models
outline.practicePrompt: Define a Pydantic model for a chat request (with fields like message: str and max_tokens: int) and use it as your FastAPI endpoint's input type.

outline.point: Async endpoints in FastAPI for calling external LLM APIs without blocking
outline.practicePrompt: Write an async FastAPI endpoint that calls a mock external API using httpx and returns the result.

outline.point: Streaming responses (for token-by-token LLM output)
outline.practicePrompt: Build a FastAPI endpoint that uses StreamingResponse to send back a sequence of words with a small delay between each, simulating token streaming.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: structured/forced JSON outputs from an LLM using Pydantic models
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why forcing an LLM to return a strict JSON structure (matching a Pydantic model) is more reliable for downstream code than parsing free-form text.

outline.point: What machine learning is: supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning at a conceptual level
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning using one example of each.

outline.point: Train/test split and why we don't evaluate a model on its training data
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why evaluating a model only on its training data gives a misleadingly optimistic sense of performance.

outline.point: Basic classification and regression concepts using scikit-learn (fit/predict workflow)
outline.practicePrompt: Train a simple scikit-learn classifier (e.g. logistic regression) on a small sample dataset and print its accuracy on a held-out test set.

outline.point: Evaluation metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix
outline.practicePrompt: Given a confusion matrix, manually calculate precision, recall, and F1-score, and explain when you'd prioritize recall over precision.

outline.point: Overfitting vs underfitting, and the bias-variance tradeoff
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the bias-variance tradeoff out loud, giving one example of a high-bias model and one example of a high-variance model.

outline.point: Regularization (L1/L2) and cross-validation as ways to control overfitting
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between L1 and L2 regularization and describe what k-fold cross-validation does.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: bagging vs boosting, and why ensemble methods often outperform single models
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between bagging (e.g. Random Forest) and boosting (e.g. gradient boosting) in your own words.

outline.point: Neural network basics: neurons, layers, activation functions, and forward pass (conceptual)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in your own words, what a neural network layer computes and why non-linear activation functions are necessary.

outline.point: NLP preprocessing basics: tokenization, stemming/lemmatization
outline.practicePrompt: Tokenize a sample sentence using a subword tokenizer (e.g. Hugging Face's AutoTokenizer) and print the resulting tokens and token IDs.

outline.point: Text representation: from TF-IDF and Word2Vec/GloVe (static embeddings) to contextual embeddings
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why 'bank' gets the same vector in Word2Vec regardless of context, but a different vector in a contextual embedding model like BERT.

outline.point: The Transformer architecture: self-attention, multi-head attention, and positional encoding
outline.practicePrompt: Explain in your own words what 'self-attention' allows a transformer to do that a simple word-by-word model cannot.

outline.point: Common NLP tasks: text classification, Named Entity Recognition (NER), sentiment analysis
outline.practicePrompt: Use a pre-trained Hugging Face pipeline to run sentiment analysis and NER on 3 sample sentences and inspect the outputs.

outline.point: Context window: what it is, why it's limited, and how it affects long-document processing
outline.practicePrompt: Explain what a context window is and describe one practical problem you'd hit if you tried to feed a 500-page document directly into a model with a small context window.

outline.point: Fine-tuning concepts: full fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/QLoRA) at a conceptual level
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, at a high level, what LoRA does differently from full fine-tuning, and why it's cheaper to run.

outline.point: What an AI Engineer does differently from an ML Engineer/Researcher (using pre-trained models vs training from scratch)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in your own words, the difference between an AI Engineer role (applying pre-trained models) and an ML Engineer/Researcher role (building and training models).

outline.point: Inference vs training: what happens when you call an LLM API
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between 'training' a model and 'running inference' on it, using an API call to GPT or Claude as the inference example.

outline.point: Popular pre-trained model families and how to compare them (OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, open-source models)
outline.practicePrompt: Pick two LLM providers (e.g. OpenAI and Anthropic) and compare their context window sizes and knowledge cutoff dates from their official documentation.

outline.point: Making your first API call: the Chat Completions pattern (system/user/assistant roles)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a Python script that calls an LLM chat completion API with a system message and a user message, and prints the response.

outline.point: Managing tokens: what a token is, maximum tokens, and basic token counting
outline.practicePrompt: Use a tokenizer library to count how many tokens a sample paragraph consumes, and estimate the API cost using the provider's per-token pricing.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: understanding and mitigating hallucination — why LLMs generate plausible but false statements
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why an LLM can generate a fluent, confident-sounding answer that is factually wrong, and name one technique (e.g. RAG) used to reduce this.

outline.point: Anatomy of a good prompt: instructions, context, examples, and output format
outline.practicePrompt: Write a system prompt for a customer-support assistant that specifies its role, tone, and the exact output format you want.

outline.point: Zero-shot vs few-shot prompting (providing example inputs/outputs)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a zero-shot prompt and a few-shot version (with 2-3 examples) for classifying customer messages as 'complaint' or 'question', and compare the outputs.

outline.point: Chain-of-Thought prompting: forcing the model to reason step by step
outline.practicePrompt: Write a math word problem prompt with and without 'let's think step by step' appended, and compare the two responses.

outline.point: Structured outputs: forcing JSON responses that match a schema
outline.practicePrompt: Write a prompt (or use structured-output/function-calling mode) that forces the model to return a JSON object with exactly the fields 'name', 'skills', and 'years_experience' from a raw resume text.

outline.point: Prompt templates and reusable prompt patterns
outline.practicePrompt: Write a reusable prompt template with placeholders (e.g. {document}, {question}) and fill it in for 3 different documents.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: prompt injection — what it is and basic defenses
outline.practicePrompt: Explain what a prompt injection attack is, using an example where a user tries to override a system prompt's instructions, and describe one defensive technique.

outline.point: Understanding AI safety issues: bias, fairness, and unsafe outputs (overview)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, with an example, how a language model can produce biased outputs even without being explicitly programmed to.

outline.point: Prompt injection attacks and adversarial testing of LLM applications
outline.practicePrompt: Describe one adversarial test you would run against a customer-support chatbot to check whether it can be tricked into leaking its system prompt.

outline.point: Using moderation tools to filter unsafe content (e.g. a moderation API)
outline.practicePrompt: Send 3 sample pieces of text (safe, borderline, and clearly unsafe) through a content moderation API and inspect the category scores returned.

outline.point: Constraining model inputs and outputs, and knowing your users/use cases before deployment
outline.practicePrompt: For a hypothetical children's education chatbot, list 3 concrete constraints you would put on both the input and the output.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: security and privacy concerns specific to LLM applications (PII leakage, data retention)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain one risk of sending user PII (personally identifiable information) directly into a third-party LLM API prompt, and one mitigation.

outline.point: What embeddings are: turning text into vectors that capture semantic meaning
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in your own words, why two semantically similar sentences end up with vectors that are close together in embedding space.

outline.point: Generating embeddings using an API (e.g. OpenAI embeddings) and open-source alternatives (Sentence Transformers)
outline.practicePrompt: Generate embeddings for 5 sample sentences using an embeddings API or a Sentence Transformers model, and print the vector dimensions.

outline.point: Measuring similarity: cosine similarity and other distance metrics
outline.practicePrompt: Compute the cosine similarity between the embeddings of 'I love pizza' and 'Pizza is my favorite food', versus 'The weather is cold today', and compare the scores.

outline.point: Use cases for embeddings: semantic search, recommendation, anomaly detection, and classification
outline.practicePrompt: Describe how you would use embeddings to build a 'find similar support tickets' feature.

outline.point: What a vector database is and why you need one at scale (vs. a plain in-memory list of vectors)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why searching a list of 10 million embeddings by brute-force cosine similarity becomes impractical, and how a vector database's indexing helps.

outline.point: Picking and using a vector database (e.g. Chroma or FAISS for local development, Pinecone/Weaviate/Qdrant for production)
outline.practicePrompt: Set up a local Chroma or FAISS vector store, insert 5 sample document embeddings, and run a similarity search query against it.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexing at a conceptual level, and trade-offs between vector DB options
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why vector databases use approximate nearest neighbor search instead of exact search for large datasets, and name one trade-off this introduces.

outline.point: Open-source vs closed-source models: trade-offs (cost, control, data privacy vs convenience)
outline.practicePrompt: List 2 reasons a company might choose an open-source model like Llama or Mistral over a closed API like GPT, and 2 reasons they might not.

outline.point: Finding and evaluating models on the Hugging Face Hub
outline.practicePrompt: Search the Hugging Face Hub for a small open-source text-classification model, and read its model card to identify its intended use case and limitations.

outline.point: Using the Hugging Face Transformers library and pipelines for common tasks
outline.practicePrompt: Load a Hugging Face pipeline for text generation and generate a completion for a sample prompt.

outline.point: Running open-source LLMs locally with Ollama
outline.practicePrompt: Install Ollama, pull a small open-source model, and send it a prompt from the command line and from a Python script.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: when to choose a hosted API vs a self-hosted open-source model for a production application
outline.practicePrompt: Argue both sides: give one scenario where a hosted API (like OpenAI) is the better choice, and one where self-hosting an open-source model makes more sense.

outline.point: What RAG is and the problem it solves (limited context, stale training data, hallucination)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in your own words, why RAG can reduce hallucinations by grounding an LLM's answer in retrieved documents, without eliminating them entirely.

outline.point: RAG vs fine-tuning: when to use which approach
outline.practicePrompt: For a company wanting a chatbot that answers questions about its constantly-changing product catalog, explain why RAG is likely a better fit than fine-tuning.

outline.point: Document ingestion and chunking strategies (fixed-size, recursive, semantic chunking)
outline.practicePrompt: Split a sample multi-paragraph document into chunks using a recursive character splitter (e.g. ~400-512 tokens with 10-20% overlap) and inspect the resulting chunks.

outline.point: Embedding and indexing chunks into a vector store
outline.practicePrompt: Embed your chunked document from the previous step and store the embeddings in a local vector database (e.g. Chroma).

outline.point: The retrieval process: similarity search and building the augmented prompt
outline.practicePrompt: Write code that takes a user question, retrieves the top-3 most relevant chunks from your vector store, and assembles them into a prompt for the LLM.

outline.point: Building an end-to-end RAG pipeline using a framework (LangChain or LlamaIndex)
outline.practicePrompt: Use LangChain's RetrievalQA (or LlamaIndex's query engine) to build a working question-answering system over a small set of documents.

outline.point: Evaluating RAG quality: coherence vs faithfulness, and why bigger context windows don't fix bad retrieval
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between a RAG answer that is 'coherent' and one that is 'faithful' to the retrieved documents, and why a system can score well on one but poorly on the other.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: designing a RAG system end-to-end in an interview (a very common 2026 AI Engineer interview question)
outline.practicePrompt: Practice a 5-minute mock answer to 'design a RAG system for our customer support product', covering ingestion, chunking, embedding, retrieval, and generation.

outline.point: What an AI agent is, and how it differs from a plain RAG/prompt-response system
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between a simple RAG chatbot and an agent that can decide which tool to call next.

outline.point: Function calling / tool calling: letting an LLM invoke external functions with structured arguments
outline.practicePrompt: Define a simple 'get_weather(city)' function schema and use an LLM's function/tool-calling feature to have it decide when to call this function based on a user message.

outline.point: The ReAct pattern: reasoning and acting in a loop (thought → action → observation)
outline.practicePrompt: Trace through, step by step, how a ReAct agent would answer 'What is the population of the capital of France?' using a search tool, writing out each thought/action/observation.

outline.point: Building a basic agent using LangChain (or LangGraph) with one or two tools
outline.practicePrompt: Build a LangChain agent with a calculator tool and a search tool, then ask it a question that requires using both.

outline.point: Agent memory: keeping track of conversation history and state across turns
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why an agent without memory would fail at a multi-turn task like 'book me a flight, then find a hotel near where I'm flying'.

outline.point: Multi-agent systems: when and why to split work across multiple specialized agents (conceptual)
outline.practicePrompt: Describe a scenario where you'd split a task across two specialized agents (e.g. a 'researcher' agent and a 'writer' agent) instead of using one agent for everything.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: agent reliability and debugging — why agents can get stuck in loops or call the wrong tool
outline.practicePrompt: Explain one common failure mode of AI agents (e.g. infinite tool-calling loops) and one design technique to guard against it (e.g. a maximum step limit).

outline.point: What containers are and why they help deploy AI applications consistently
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in your own words, the problem containers solve (the 'it works on my machine' problem).

outline.point: Writing a basic Dockerfile for a Python/FastAPI application
outline.practicePrompt: Write a Dockerfile that packages your FastAPI app from the REST APIs topic, and build the image locally.

outline.point: Building and running a container, and exposing ports
outline.practicePrompt: Run your built Docker image, map it to a local port, and confirm you can call your API endpoint from the host machine.

outline.point: Environment variables and managing secrets (e.g. API keys) in containers
outline.practicePrompt: Modify your Dockerfile/run command to pass an API key as an environment variable instead of hardcoding it in your source code.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: basic understanding of CI/CD pipelines and why they matter for shipping AI services
outline.practicePrompt: Explain in your own words what a CI/CD pipeline automates, and why automated testing matters more, not less, for AI-powered features.

outline.point: Why AI applications are deployed to the cloud: scalability, managed services, GPU access
outline.practicePrompt: Explain one reason a startup would choose a managed cloud AI service instead of running everything on their own laptop or server.

outline.point: Overview of managed AI services (e.g. AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI Service) vs calling a provider's API directly
outline.practicePrompt: Explain one advantage of using a managed service like AWS Bedrock to access an LLM instead of calling the model provider's API directly.

outline.point: Deploying a containerized app to a basic cloud compute service
outline.practicePrompt: Deploy the Docker image you built earlier to a free-tier cloud compute service and confirm you can reach it over the internet.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: basic cost/performance trade-offs of cloud AI deployment (latency, cost per token, GPU vs CPU)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, at a high level, why running inference on a GPU instance is usually faster but more expensive than a CPU instance, and when the trade-off is worth it.

outline.point: Why evaluating an LLM application is harder than evaluating a traditional classifier (no single 'correct' output)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why you can't just check 'exact match' to evaluate whether an LLM's summary of an article is good.

outline.point: Common evaluation metrics for RAG: context relevance, faithfulness/groundedness, answer relevance
outline.practicePrompt: For a sample RAG answer and its retrieved documents, manually assess whether the answer is 'faithful' (every claim traceable to a document) and explain your reasoning.

outline.point: Using an evaluation framework (e.g. Ragas) to score RAG pipeline outputs
outline.practicePrompt: Run a small evaluation framework on 3 sample question-answer-context triples from your RAG pipeline and inspect the faithfulness/relevance scores.

outline.point: Observability basics: logging prompts, responses, latency, and token usage in production
outline.practicePrompt: Add logging to your FastAPI LLM endpoint that records the prompt, response, latency, and token count for each request.

outline.point: Tracing tools for debugging multi-step chains/agents (e.g. LangSmith-style tracing)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain what a 'trace' of an agent's execution shows you, and why this is more useful for debugging than just looking at the final output.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: what 'observability in LLM' means and why teams add it before scaling a GenAI feature
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in your own words, what observability means for an LLM-powered application and give one metric you would monitor in production.

outline.point: Number systems, percentages, and ratio/proportion basics
outline.practicePrompt: Solve 5 mixed percentage and ratio word problems within 10 minutes, timing yourself.

outline.point: Profit, loss, discount, and simple/compound interest problems
outline.practicePrompt: Solve 5 profit-and-loss and interest word problems, then re-derive each formula from first principles instead of memorizing it.

outline.point: Time, speed, distance and time & work problems
outline.practicePrompt: Solve 5 time-speed-distance problems and 5 time-and-work problems under a strict 15-minute timer.

outline.point: Permutations, combinations, and basic probability
outline.practicePrompt: Solve 3 permutation/combination problems and 3 basic probability problems.

outline.point: Logical reasoning: number/letter series, coding-decoding, seating arrangements
outline.practicePrompt: Solve 3 number-series puzzles, 2 coding-decoding puzzles, and one seating-arrangement puzzle, checking answers against explanations afterward.

outline.point: Timed mock-test strategy for section-locked tests (TCS/Infosys/Accenture-style written rounds)
outline.practicePrompt: Take one 20-minute mock aptitude section and afterward write down which question types you should skip-and-return-to next time to save time.
